target_customer: Academic and industry scientists, later pharma and biotech R&D and procurement teams, who outsource experiments and services to suppliers
problem: Scientists lacked a simple way to find, vet, contract and pay specialized labs and core facilities, so expensive equipment sat idle in one place while researchers elsewhere could not access it.
business_model: Marketplace taking a fee on outsourced research orders, evolving into enterprise software for supplier management with payments
product_category: Scientific services marketplace and R&D procurement software

founders.name: Elizabeth Iorns
prior_employers: University of Miami Miller School of Medicine (assistant professor, 2011)
founders.background_notes: Wikipedia says she was an assistant professor at Miami in 2011. Education not stated in opened sources.

founders.name: Dan Knox
founders.background_notes: Named as co-founder by Wikipedia and TechCrunch; not on the YC page.

founders.name: Ryan Abbott
founders.background_notes: Named as co-founder by Wikipedia; not on the YC page or TechCrunch.

competitors.name: Assay Depot (later Scientist.com)
competitors.what: Outsourcing marketplace for drug discovery services, launched September 2008; earns subscription fees from vendors

technical_complexity.rationale: A marketplace with vendor profiles, quoting, ordering and escrow style payments is standard web engineering; the hard part was supply side onboarding and quality, not technology.

defensibility.rationale: A network of thousands of vetted suppliers and an enterprise master service agreement and payments integration created lock in, though early on Assay Depot offered a similar marketplace.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent copied it. Science Exchange bought OnDeckBiotech in 2016, was itself acquired by Waud Capital Partners on 2024-09-30, and bought HappiLabs in March 2025.

market_need_then: TechCrunch in August 2011 described a central marketplace for core research facilities. Academic and industry labs spent heavily on outsourced experiments and core facilities, while the market for finding them was fragmented.

identity.voice_and_tone: Mission driven, science focused; early press framed it as eBay for science

branding.brand_signature: Reproducibility Initiative launched with PLOS in August 2012
branding.community_and_virality: The 2012 Reproducibility Initiative with PLOS and later reproducibility work with the Center for Open Science raised its profile in the science community.

brand_strength.rationale: Recognized among life science buyers and covered by Scientific American and trade press, but a descriptive name with no sourced evidence of a distinctive mascot or style.

pivots.from: Marketplace for academic researchers and core facilities
pivots.to: Enterprise platform for big pharma R&D outsourcing
pivots.why: TechCrunch headline for the Series B said it moved into big pharma; reasoning beyond that not opened

outcome_analysis: Science Exchange built a marketplace of vetted research suppliers, raised a seed from Andreessen Horowitz, a Series A from Union Square Ventures, a $25 million Series B in 2016 and a $28 million Series C in 2017, and moved upmarket to pharma procurement software. It was acquired by Waud Capital Partners on 2024-09-30 after raising roughly $98 million to $100 million by aggregator counts, with terms undisclosed.
notes: Series A amount conflicts: Wikipedia says $4M, a cited source says $3M; $4M recorded. Wikipedia states the 2011 pre-seed pieces and Dec 2011 seed; the seed is also listed by an aggregator (startupintros). 2019 round described as equity plus debt. Business Wire release for the Waud deal returned HTTP 403 but the company's press page and several outlets in search results confirm it; terms not disclosed. Founders' education not found. The current company website mentions no acquisition and no leadership. Competitor source is from Nov 2012, about 15 months after founding; Assay Depot launched in 2008 so it existed at founding.
